TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
MONDAY, 20 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 10:01 AM (AEST)
DAY 32
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MR DOUGLAS FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth
MR NICHOLAS ANDREATIDIS KC, for Mr Charles Wann
MR MIN GUO, for Ms Katherine Prygodicz and Ms Felicity Button

COMMISSIONER: Here we are for the fourth set of hearings. I will just indicate that my plan
for the moment is to stick to regular inquiry hours of 10 until 1, 2.30 until 4.30, until we start
getting in trouble with the witness list, in which case we will adapt accordingly. Yes,
Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you, Commissioner. This morning I appear with Mr Freeburn of
Counsel. This afternoon I will appear with Ms Berry of Counsel.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear today with Mr Glover of Counsel for the
Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Mr Andreatidis?
MR ANDREATIDIS: Good morning. I appear instructed by King & Wood Mallesons for
Mr Wann, who is number 5 on the list today, Commissioner. Can I be - - -
COMMISSIONER: What's a not-before time for Mr - - -
MR GREGGERY: Ms Lees and Mr Wann are unlikely to be reached before lunch, so not before
2.30.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Are you confident about that?
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And can you leave a phone number just in case anything moves faster, to
be on the safe side. But otherwise, not before 2.30.
MR ANDREATIDIS: Of course. Thank you. May I be excused?
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Thanks.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. The fourth Public hearing of the Royal
Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, of course, commences today for a period of three
weeks, concluding on Friday, 10 March 2023. It is planned to be the final Public hearing. The
list of witnesses was published on the Commission's website and reflects the substantial
body of oral evidence on a range of topics, which is anticipated will be given during this
hearing. The broad overview of those topics was also updated on the website. Those topics
reveal the Commission's continued interest into critical points in time where decisions to
implement, continue and ultimately wind up the Scheme were made.

The evidence is expected to focus on who knew what and when about the four-year Budget
Measure which came to be known as the Robodebt Scheme. It will also focus on why critical
information was not communicated to decision-makers, or if it was, why it was not
communicated outside of the relevant Departments. The evidence is also anticipated to
include why those in positions of seniority made decisions to implement or continue the
Scheme despite their knowledge of flaws and in the face of public scrutiny, independent
investigations and legal challenges.
Last week, the Attorney-General announced the extension of the due date for the delivery of
the report of this Commission's inquiry into the matters set out in the Terms of Reference.
The due date is now 30 June 2023. The extension reflects the significant work needed to
address the Terms of Reference and the extraordinary volume of material produced in
response to the various notices issued by the Commission. By way of example, during the last
Hearing Block, which commenced only a month ago, over 100,000 additional documents
were produced. That fact and the extension further illustrates what I said in my opening
address, that much of the work of the Commission involves the analysis of documents and
evidence which is undertaken outside of these Public hearings.
Two documents were produced which have not previously been tendered. They are to be
Exhibits 5106A and 5107. It's convenient at this point, Commissioner, if I tender the list of
exhibits - or tender the exhibits listed in the draft list for the whole day. It commences at
5106A and concludes at 5268.
COMMISSIONER: Exhibits 5106A through to 5268, as listed in the exhibit list, are admitted.
<EXHIBITS 5106A TO 5268 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
MR GREGGERY: The two documents to which I have just referred which had not previously
been tendered are directly relevant to the question of the advice received by the
Department of Human Services at a point during the Scheme. And I call at this point for
Exhibit 5106A to be placed on the screen. Commissioner, you may recall evidence that
Ms Musolino as Chief Counsel of DHS sent an email to all legal departments on 23 January
2017, and it is contained there in the bottom half of that page. And it sought identification
and provision of legal advices, whether internal or external, provided by Legal to the
business regarding debt recovery of Centrelink overpayments.
In response to that request by Ms Musolino to the various persons listed as recipients to that
email, Mr Glyn Fiveash produced document 5107. And I would ask that that be placed on the
screen. And it was produced, as that first document indicated, on the same day. Mr Fiveash
communicated to Ms Musolino that he wrote this, which he described as an information
piece for the strategic analysis section, a couple of weeks earlier. The language of the advice
addresses the question of debts, as is identified in the subtitle. And in the first paragraph,
Mr Fiveash identifies two stages of assessment of entitlement, the first when a person
receives an income support supplement and the second in respect of the question of
whether there had been an overpayment.

In the second paragraph, which is of direct relevance to the inquiry, Mr Fiveash provides
advice to the recipient about the question of whether averaging may be used, and he arrives
at a position which is set out in the last five lines where he concludes, that is:
The Department cannot apply an income amount received over a larger period, for example,
12 months, in any way against a customer other than the manner in which the person
received it in those individual fortnights.
And the explanation is given there. He concludes:
Rather, the annual amount needs to be apportioned between the relevant fortnights in the
period at the rate at which it was actually earned, derived or received.
The use of the word "apportioned" in the final sentence has been used in a different context
throughout this inquiry, and the emphasis in the full context of the advice on the last
sentence is the word "actually". Mr Fiveash refers to the critical factual point about when
income was earned, derived or received, rather than the concept of averaging which is set
out above
That, properly understood, was an advice that averaged income could not be used to
calculate debts by the Department. It is not clear what - or, rather, the evidence does not yet
reveal what Ms Musolino did with that advice after receiving it on 23 January 2017, and part
of the oral evidence to be given during the course of this hearing I expect will involve
questioning of Ms Musolino on that topic. The document can be taken down.
Additional questions in - under the broad category of legal advice have been the subject of
discussions between Solicitors Assisting the Commonwealth and Solicitors Assisting the
Commission in recent months. They fall into two categories. the first is the question of
whether the Commonwealth considers that it has waived, or will waive, legal professional
privilege in respect of the advice from the Australian Government Solicitor on constitutional
risk for the purpose of the New Policy Proposal which was considered by the Expenditure
Review Committee on 25 March 2015.
The Commonwealth position, I understand - and a letter will be produced to this
effect - contends that it has not waived and will not waive privilege in the constitutional risk
advice. The consequence of that position - and Solicitors Assisting the Commission are
considering it - is that in that specific respect, this Commission will not be able to address the
question of the nature of the advice received by the Commonwealth in respect of the Budget
Measure. However, there are discussions in play which may reveal a portion of the advice
without leading to the ultimate conclusion. That is a matter which the solicitors, as I said,
continue to correspond on.
The second category of legal advice which has been the subject of a correspondence
between the solicitors is the Australian Government Solicitor advice in respect of how
persons who were prosecuted after having debts raised which involve the use of averaging
ought be treated in respect of the categories of persons identified in the class action - or,

understand, is writing to Solicitors Assisting the Commission to inform them that similarly to
the Constitutional risk assessment advice, the Commonwealth maintains legal professional
privilege in respect of the AGS advice about what I might describe as the fraud cohort.
That question has had relevance to some witnesses, particularly Mr Carter from the DPP. The
Commission might recall that I reserved tender of a category of documents, and there are
witnesses tomorrow to whom that question is relevant. But in view of the volume of material
today and the evolving situation, it's not relevant to seek a ruling in that respect at this point.
It may be necessary to raise it again tomorrow upon receipt of correspondence. I simply flag
it at this point. But again, in the event that the Commonwealth proceeds in the manner that
it has foreshadowed to me and which I have just outlined, the Commission will not be in a
position to address that category of the Term of Reference which deals with advice received
by the Commonwealth in respect of the Scheme and the response to legal challenges.
If I turn, then, to the topic of submissions. The Commission has received more than 1,000
submissions from various people over the course of the Commission so far. Those
submissions fall into two broad categories: those who experienced the Robodebt Scheme
either personally, including those who worked at Centrelink, DHS or DSS, or through family
members or who have direct personal experience which they have shared with others; and,
secondly, those whose qualifications, work experience or profession allows them to make
submissions which assist the Commission to identify flaws in the Scheme, reasons why
existing checks and balances were unable to halt the Scheme and recommendations to avoid
the repetition of what may appear on the evidence so far and without any concluded view,
of course, of the apparently systemic issues involved in establishing and maintaining the
Scheme.
I anticipate that the submissions falling into the second category, broadly described as expert
submissions, will be able to be tendered later this week. The Commission has also engaged
three persons who fall into that category of experts to produce reports which will assist the
Commission. Dr Elea Wurth, who is listed on the witness list for the third week of this
Hearing Block, and Deloitte have been engaged to provide expert advice on the design and
implementation of the Scheme. That advice will be provided by way of detailed process maps
of the way that data was transmitted between DHS and the ATO, and the way the data was
used at DHS to raise debts during the period of the Scheme, and a report to the Royal
Commission.
The report will address the following questions: the technical end-to-end Scheme process as
it pertains to the automation of employment PAYG compliance program delivered across
DHS and the ATO, including population identification, identity matching, income matching,
debt calculation and debt notification - I pause there. A number of the expert submissions
received in the broad category that I identified earlier include submissions in respect of
automated decision-making and the use of artificial intelligence in decision-making.
The report will also address whether the activities undertaken by DHS appear to differ from
the requirements outlined in the agency's framework documents; what governance controls
and risk management instruments were in place between and within DHS and ATO to ensure

documents; whether the governance controls, risk management instruments identified were
sufficient; to what extent and in what steps the PAYG Income Compliance Program was
automated; and what steps could be taken in future data matching programs to improve two
features, first, governance, risk management and controls for income data matching to
improve compliance with legislative instruments and protocols and, second, trustworthy
automation to improve compliance in the same way and adherence to the values of the
Australian Public Service.
Ms Wurth has been briefed with hundreds of primary documents produced to the
Commission for the purpose of this engagement. I can indicate that the ATO and Services
Australia were provided with the process maps last week, and we are awaiting their
response in that respect. It appears from the information provided to the Commission to
date that Ms Wurth's analysis of the end-to-end program is the first of its type despite the
systems being established in 2015 and 2016.
The second expert engaged by the Commission is Professor Whiteford. He has been engaged
to provide a report in relation to patterns of employment and earnings of income support
recipients at the time of the introduction and application of the Robodebt Scheme, including
a review of data and analysis being produced to the Commission by the Department of Social
Services. And the Commission may recall the observations of Justice Murphy in the reasons
for the settlement of the class action, which referred to what might ought reasonably be
expected to be known by the Departments about those who were in receipt of those
benefits.
And his report will address a number of critical features: whether the use of data based on
the assumption that a recipient's income can be averaged over an annual period to identify
overpayments is consistent with policy directions in the social security system with respect
to encouraging work by benefit recipients; changes in the employment patterns and income
patterns of income support recipients in the period 2010 to 2015, prior to the introduction of
the Scheme, and in 2015 to 2019, during the Scheme; patterns of interaction of income
support recipients with the social security system in the period 2010 to 2019; the nature of
the labour market and work opportunities for low income earners and income support
recipients in that same period; and in light of those characteristics, whether the assumptions
underlying income averaging, that is, that incomes are consistently earned with little
variation between fortnights, could be regarded as reasonably accurate or as reasonably
reliable indicators of fortnightly income; and whether any concerns identified in relation to
income averaging would or should have been identifiable in 2015 based on the information
available at that time about the employment and income patterns of recipients.
The third expert is Mr Podger, a former Public Service Commissioner, to provide a report
which addresses certain questions which arise for consideration from the Terms of Reference
and evidence to date. His report will address the role of the Australian Public Service and the
professional relationship that exists or existed between public service leaders and their
agency Ministers, and their respective responsibilities; the responsibilities of individual public
servants, particularly Secretaries of Department and those in the Senior Executive Service
and Executive Level, including their statutory obligations under the Public Service Act 1999

Disclosure Act of 2010; for the relevant period of the Scheme, the relationship between the
policy advising and administration, as well as the structure of the social security portfolio,
that is, the respective roles of and relationships between the Department of Social Security,
Social Services and Services Australia; the annual Budget process and Mid-Year Economic
Forecast process arrangements for ensuring Cabinet had sufficient information, including on
legal and other risks, to make proper decisions; the relationship and level of engagement
between Services Australia and DSS, and each agency's clients and stakeholders; the use of
technology in the administration of social security payments, including data matching and
automated decision-making; the role of compliance and the appropriate balance between
compliance and the proper administration of beneficial legislation, particularly the social
security laws; the level of APS capabilities within the social security portfolio, including with
regard to policy advice, administrative experience, understanding of social security and
administrative law and project management; the question of the culture of Services Australia
and DSS, and the levels of communication between the two agencies; quality of
recordkeeping within the Australian Public Service, as it has been identified in this
Commission; and his recommendations to address any concerns which he identifies which
appear to him to be systemic and any concerns identified in respect of critical points in the
Scheme. Each of these reports are being finalised, and I expect that they will be tendered
later this week.
I turn, then, to the question of evidence today. Commissioner, the evidence today will
commence with Ms Miller, whose son Rhys Cauzzo committed suicide on 26 January 2017
after debts were generated using averaging in the PAYG Manual Compliance Intervention
process during the 2015-2016 financial year. After the morning break - and I expect, of
course, Ms Miller will take us to that point - Ms Prygodicz and Ms Button will give evidence
as a panel of their personal experience with the Scheme and their conjoint experience as
lead applicants in the class action.
And this afternoon, as I indicated earlier, Ms Lees, the former Chief of Staff to Senator Payne
in 2015, and Mr Wann, former Chief of Staff to Mr Morrison in 2015, will give evidence of
their role insofar as it is relevant to the implementation of the Scheme and their respective
Ministers' knowledge of the development of the Scheme and attendance at the Expenditure
Review Committee on 25 March 2015 when the measure was approved. It is convenient,
then, if Ms Miller be called.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Ms Miller. Now, having got you sat down, I'm going to ask you to stand
up again. Would you rather take an oath or an affirmation?
MS MILLER: Affirmation. Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: All right. We will get that administered. Thank you.
<JENNIFER JOY MILLER, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY

MR GREGGERY: Yes. For the record, I can indicate that Ms Miller is supported by her partner,
who is present, and is also represented, and her representative is present in the Commission
room should the situation arise. Ms Miller, can you tell the Commission your full name,
please?
MS MILLER: Jennifer Joy Miller. Can you hear us?
COMMISSIONER: Well, I can, but do you think there's a - - -
MR GREGGERY: I can't see a microphone as is usually the case, but - - -
COMMISSIONER: Ms Hogan-Doran, you always notice if there is a problem. Can you hear Ms
Miller all right?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I think the problem is that my microphone was on. It is now off, and
hopefully that improves everything. I think my microphone was on, which may have been
picking up ambience.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Okay. Right. All right. So let's try again.
MR GREGGERY: Ms Miller, you have provided a Statement dated 17 February 2023 to this
Commission?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And it sets out in some detail what you now know as a result of viewing
various documents produced to the Commission which had been tendered earlier today?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And your knowledge relates to your son, Rhys Cauzzo?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And your involvement in communications with various government entities,
both State and Commonwealth, over the last five years?
MS MILLER: Yes - six years, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you. You are the mother of two boys, Ms Miller?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And Rhys was the younger of those two?

MR GREGGERY: He passed away on 26 January 2017.
MS MILLER: Yes, that's right.
MR GREGGERY: How did you come to know or learn of that?
MS MILLER: The police arrived to our house at 3 o'clock in the morning and delivered the
news that Rhys had passed. The reason that they came to the property was because of social
media. They were worried that maybe I would have seen something on social media about it
before I knew about anything. So, yes.
MR GREGGERY: At the time, you were living in Queensland?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you still do?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And prior to his death, where did Rhys live?
MS MILLER: Rhys was living in Cairns, but he was living in Melbourne from 2009.
MR GREGGERY: And he had lived in Melbourne from 2009 through to January 2017?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You came to learn that Rhys received letters alleging debts in late 2016.
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And if we jump forward a number of years to 2020 and 2021, did you come
to learn that moneys recovered from Rhys by the Department of Human Services prior to his
death were refunded to him?
MS MILLER: Yes, that's right.
MR GREGGERY: And the debts that were alleged against him in late 2016 and continuing in
January 2017 were zeroed, to use the term - - -
MS MILLER: Yes. That's right.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. When you learned of your son's death, what did you do?
MS MILLER: The first 24 hours was fairly hazy. But I immediately had a plane booked to fly

property where he was living and - which was the - the next afternoon. And I was frantically
searching for him - leaving a note or a - something - some explanation. And - because it
didn't feel right. It - I just knew it wasn't just, like, a simple reason, I suppose. So whilst I was
going through all the property, I also collated any material that I - may be necessary for me
to follow up on. And then on the fridge, I found the debt letters from Dun & Bradstreet and a
picture of Rhys with a gun to his head. Yes. So - when I saw that, I knew that something
wasn't right.
MR GREGGERY: You say Dun & Bradstreet. Did you come to learn that a debt collection
agency, Dun & Bradstreet, had been assigned by the Department of Human Services to
pursue Rhys in respect of the debts alleged by the Department?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And do you recall how many of those letters were on the fridge?
MS MILLER: There was five letters, and I thought it was like a business card that had been left
there, but it was like a sticky - sticky note that had been left - easy-peel, I think they call it.
Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And was it your understanding at that time that this note was something left
by the debt collector, Dun & Bradstreet - - -
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: - - - asking Rhys to contact them?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And had been delivered to the house at some point?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Before I move on to the other document that you found, was Rhys living
alone at the time?
MS MILLER: He was living with his partner - - -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS MILLER: - - - and also a friend. So - and they had been out all day, and [REDACTED] had
gone out to go and get some cheesecake, and she came back and found Rhys.
MR GREGGERY: Now, the drawing that you found, what type of drawing was it?
MS MILLER: It was a face with a gun through there and dollar signs just coming out of his

MR GREGGERY: When had you last seen Rhys?
MS MILLER: I had been down in the first week of June. Towards the end of May, Rhys had
rung me, and he was really, really quite stressed. And so I said to him, "I will come down.
Let's, you know, sort some things out.” He said, "I've got a debt letter. I - can't be right, can't
be right.” And so I flew down in the June. And I spent some time with Rhys to get him back
on track and thinking clearly and helping him. Unbeknownst to me, he - he didn't actually let
me know how much pressure he was starting to feel from the debts and - plus, we didn't
know anything about Robodebt. So it was like, no, this can't be real. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And do you recall the amounts of the debts that you and Rhys talked about
when you visited him in mid-2016?
MS MILLER: The first debt letters that I saw was for around $10,300. And then the next one
included an extra debt that I thought was a separate debt, and that was 17,000-something.
MR GREGGERY: And did you later come to learn that the 17,000-odd figure was a
combination of two alleged debts?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Right. You say Rhys hadn't discussed the full extent of the impact of the
debts on him when you spoke to him in - I think it was May 2016.
MS MILLER: Yes, end of May.
MR GREGGERY: End of May. And that is when you visited him in Melbourne?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: But he indicated to you that there was some effect upon him in respect of
the debts?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And is that what prompted you to go and visit him?
MS MILLER: I would go down and see Rhys as often as I could, and - but, yes, he was very
distraught when he made that phone call to me. And - and he said he was feeling suicidal.
And so we probably spoke for about two hours on the phone, maybe longer. And I said,
"Okay. I'm going to come down. Let's set up a program for you to go back to the doctor, back
to the psychologist, and let's get - get you, you know, under review," so that I could manage
him, and he could manage himself. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: How long did you stay with Rhys and his partner?

MS MILLER: It was for about five days.
MR GREGGERY: The indication of what you've just said is that Rhys did have pre-existing
mental ill health?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Before we come to that in detail, you said that he was in Cairns for a
period - the family lived in Cairns. Is that where he went to school?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: What can you tell the Commission about his last few years of school?
MS MILLER: We started seeing some signs of him having anxiety and so forth. But, you know,
to be honest, we probably didn't really think that there was something going on mentally.
And - but, you know, he had a great group of friends. He was doing okay at school, if he set
his mind to it.
MR GREGGERY: Like most boys.
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes. He would - he finished year 12. He was very creative, and all his mates
had their own band. They would do skits. They would - yes, they - they had a good time. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And when it came to the decision to leave Cairns and go to Melbourne, how
did that come about?
MS MILLER: The boys all decided that they wanted to have the music vibe and the artistic
vibe that happens in Melbourne, and - and - yes. So they got very involved in playing music at
different pubs and what have you. Rhys would do the artwork for many of the bands for
their posters and - yes. Very creative.
MR GREGGERY: What did you learn of his employment once he moved to Melbourne after
finishing grade 12?
MS MILLER: Look, initially, all the boys were probably couch surfing and doing whatever. And
ultimately, they did all settle down and find places to rent or share with. And Rhys did spend
a bit of time with my husband's family down in Melbourne as well, and he did work. He
worked always on a casual basis, and he was working for Museum Victoria as a
photographer. And then he was working as a florist for quite a number of years.
MR GREGGERY: You indicated earlier that he was artistic, and that obviously extended to
photography?
MS MILLER: Yes.

MS MILLER: Yes. Yes. He had commenced casual work when in Cairns, and that was after
school and weekends. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: So he had at least two employers at various times?
MS MILLER: He would have had - in his time in Victoria?
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS MILLER: I think there was three or four. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you said you understood that it was always casual work?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Okay. Did you talk to him about his finances periodically and how he was
going?
MS MILLER: Yes. Yes. And if he did need assistance, we would all help him out, you know,
like, "I can't pay my rego this week.” "Okay. I will pay it for you.” But he wasn't - both boys
weren't, like, relying on us for finance. It's just that sometimes they, you know, are boys.
MR GREGGERY: Following Rhys passing, you were involved in the funeral arrangements?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And did you come to meet his employer at the florist?
MS MILLER: Yes, yes.
MR GREGGERY: What did they tell you about Rhys as a worker?
MS MILLER: They adored Rhys. He was highly respected by everyone he worked with. And
they were shocked, as we all were. But he was - he was reliable. They could always count on
him to be there at work when he was required, and to the point - with his funeral, Vasette
set up the most beautiful display on behalf of Rhys. And all his previous employers and those
from Vasette, they all attended his funeral.
MR GREGGERY: Did you have - or do you recall your first engagement with the Department
of Human Services or Centrelink after Rhys's passing?
MS MILLER: I - after the funeral - so I had stayed in Melbourne for a good month. So after the
funeral, I rang Centrelink. That would have been the 13th of February, and - to advise them
of Rhys's passing. I was on hold for 57 minutes and then I was told, "Well, we - I can't input
the information. The computers are down," or something. And - and, of course, I wasn't

was a bit of a - that stirred me up quite a bit, because I certainly didn't get really any
response from them. And I asked them if they could advise Dun & Bradstreet, and they said,
"No, you've got to do that yourself.”
MR GREGGERY: So following that telephone call with Centrelink, you telephoned Dun &
Bradstreet?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And informed them that Rhys had passed?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Have you had the opportunity to listen to a recording of your phone call?
MS MILLER: I probably wouldn't like to listen to a recording of that phone call.
MR GREGGERY: Do you recall it was very distressing?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: The first that you became aware of Rhys's debts, as you have said, was in
May 2016.
MS MILLER: Yes. For the initials, yes.
MR GREGGERY: For the initial stage, yes. And one of the documents that you have referred
to is Exhibit 5186. It's a Facebook post of Rhys. Do you recall that?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: I will ask if that can be put onto the screen, please. And this is the particular
post that we can see, May 25, 2016:
Any Social Service people around?
Can you see that?
MS MILLER: Yes, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: That's a post by Rhys where he says:

Got a huge debt notice from Centrelink which I believe is incorrect, but not too sure how to go
against it since my proof (pay documents, etcetera) are long gone from five-plus years ago.
Help.
Do you see that?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. If that could be taken down. Did he express a similar sentiment
to you when you visited him later that month?
MS MILLER: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And did you understand that he had been asked to provide payslips from
many years earlier?
MS MILLER: I didn't realise it was going back that far, and it's only through the documents
I've seen now that they had raised certain debts over certain years. So when - because, like I
